"title": "Robust Brain State Decoding using Bidirectional Long Short Term Memory Networks in functional MRI",
"authors": "Anant Mittal, Priya Aggarwal, Luiz Pessoa, Anubha Gupta",
"field_subfield": "Neuroimaging / Machine Learning",
"type_of_paper": "Empirical study",
"executive_summary": "This paper addresses the challenge of decoding brain states from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data by exploiting temporal information. The authors argue that conventional Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models, which only capture past temporal context, are insufficient because of the inherent latency and dynamics of the Blood Oxygen Level Dependent (BOLD) response. They propose using a Bidirectional LSTM (bi-LSTM) that captures information from both past and future time instances, eliminating the need for delay adjustment. The study was conducted on working memory task fMRI data from the Human Connectome Project (HCP), involving 400 participants selected from a release of 1200. The data was preprocessed using HCP's pipeline, including motion regression and cortical parcellation into 360 regions of interest (ROIs). The bi-LSTM architecture consisted of two hidden layers with 256 hidden activations each, followed by a fully-connected layer with 9 neurons for softmax classification. The model was trained using inter-subject 10-fold cross-validation, with data windowed into overlapping segments of 40 time points. Training was performed on a GeForce GTX 980 GPU using the Keras framework, the ADAM optimizer, and a learning rate of 0.001 for 100 epochs. To handle class imbalance, class weights were computed using Sklearn's routine. The results showed that the bi-LSTM model achieved an overall accuracy of 0.84 ± 0.02, significantly outperforming the unidirectional LSTM, which achieved 0.66 ± 0.18. This represents an 18% improvement in accuracy. The authors conclude that the bi-LSTM model robustly predicts brain states without delay adjustment, highlighting the importance of future temporal context in capturing BOLD dynamics. The study also identifies areas for future work, such as tuning window size and overlap, and more sophisticated handling of class imbalance.",

"title": "Robust Brain State Decoding using Bidirectional Long Short Term Memory Networks in functional MRI",
"authors": "Anant Mittal, Priya Aggarwal, Luiz Pessoa, Anubha Gupta",

"type_of_paper": "Empirical study (methodological + experimental)",
"executive_summary": "This paper addresses brain-state decoding from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data, where the goal is to infer the cognitive state underlying neural activity. The authors argue that conventional decoding methods, including unidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, fail to capture the full temporal dynamics of the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) response because they only use past information. Since BOLD responses are slow and exhibit latency, the authors contend that future temporal context is equally important. To address this, they propose a bidirectional LSTM (bi-LSTM) architecture that processes the input sequence in both forward and reverse temporal orders, collating the two hidden activations to build a richer memory representation. This approach explicitly models BOLD dynamics without requiring any delay adjustment for stimulus-response synchronization. The study validates the method on working memory task fMRI data from the Human Connectome Project (HCP), using 400 participants selected from a release of 1200. Participants performed a 2-back working memory task alongside a 0-back control condition, with stimuli drawn from four categories. Each scan yielded a 405 time-point sequence of 360 cortical regions of interest. The data was preprocessed using HCP's pipeline, including motion regression and low-frequency signal removal, and parcellated into 360 ROIs. The bi-LSTM was implemented in Keras and trained on a GeForce GTX 980 GPU with an ADAM optimizer, learning rate of 0.001, batch size of 32, and 100 epochs, with dropout of 0.3 to prevent overfitting. Class imbalance was handled using Sklearn's compute_class_weight routine. The model was evaluated using inter-subject 10-fold cross-validation, with the development set further split into 80-20 training-validation sets. The full-length training data was windowed into overlapping windows of size 40 with an overlap of 10 points. The results showed that the bi-LSTM (specifically the vector concatenation variant, bi-LSTM-c) achieved an overall accuracy of 0.84 ± 0.02, compared to 0.66 ± 0.18 for the unidirectional LSTM, representing an 18% improvement in accuracy. The authors note that the model performs well without hard-coded delay adjustment, highlighting the usefulness of immediate future samples. They also acknowledge limitations, including the need for more sophisticated handling of class imbalance and potential confusion between certain stimuli categories such as body and tools. Future work may involve tuning the window size and overlap for time-series chunking, as well as studying cortical regions engaged in specific stimuli. The study contributes to the field of brain-computer interfaces and cognitive decoding by demonstrating that bidirectional temporal modeling significantly improves brain-state decoding accuracy.",

summary.title: Robust Brain State Decoding using Bidirectional Long Short Term Memory Networks in functional MRI
summary.authors: Anant Mittal, Priya Aggarwal, Luiz Pessoa, Anubha Gupta
summary.executive_summary: This paper addresses brain-state decoding from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data, where the goal is to infer the cognitive state underlying neural activity. The authors argue that conventional decoding methods, including unidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, fail to capture the full temporal dynamics of the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) response because they only use past information. Since BOLD responses are slow and exhibit latency, the authors contend that future temporal context is equally important. To address this, they propose a bidirectional LSTM (bi-LSTM) architecture that processes the input sequence in both forward and reverse temporal orders, collating the two hidden activations to build a richer memory representation. This approach explicitly models BOLD dynamics without requiring any delay adjustment for stimulus-response synchronization. The study validates the method on working memory task fMRI data from the Human Connectome Project (HCP), using 400 participants selected from a release of 1200. Participants performed a 2-back working memory task alongside a 0-back control condition, with stimuli drawn from four categories. Each scan yielded a 405 time-point sequence of 360 cortical regions of interest. The data was preprocessed using HCP's pipeline, including motion regression and low-frequency signal removal, and parcellated into 360 ROIs. The bi-LSTM was implemented in Keras and trained on a GeForce GTX 980 GPU with an ADAM optimizer, learning rate of 0.001, batch size of 32, and 100 epochs, with dropout of 0.3 to prevent overfitting. Class imbalance was handled using Sklearn's compute_class_weight routine. The model was evaluated using inter-subject 10-fold cross-validation, with the development set further split into 80-20 training-validation sets. The full-length training data was windowed into overlapping windows of size 40 with an overlap of 10 points. The results showed that the bi-LSTM (specifically the vector concatenation variant, bi-LSTM-c) achieved an overall accuracy of 0.84 ± 0.02, compared to 0.66 ± 0.18 for the unidirectional LSTM, representing an 18% improvement in accuracy. The authors note that the model performs well without hard-coded delay adjustment, highlighting the usefulness of immediate future samples. They also acknowledge limitations, including the need for more sophisticated handling of class imbalance and potential confusion between certain stimuli categories such as body and tools. Future work may involve tuning the window size and overlap for time-series chunking, as well as studying cortical regions engaged in specific stimuli. The study contributes to the field of brain-computer interfaces and cognitive decoding by demonstrating that bidirectional temporal modeling significantly improves brain-state decoding accuracy.

The full-length training data was windowed into overlapping windows of size 40 with an overlap of 10 points. Future work may involve tuning the window size and overlap for time-series chunking, as well as studying cortical regions engaged in specific stimuli. The study contributes to the field of brain-computer interfaces and cognitive decoding by demonstrating that bidirectional temporal modeling significantly improves brain-state decoding accuracy.

Research Context
Brain-state decoding aims to infer cognitive processes from fMRI data. Temporal dynamics of BOLD responses are crucial but often ignored. Conventional methods rely on univariate analysis of individual voxels. Multivariate methods integrate distributed information across space. Recurrent networks like LSTM model temporal dynamics well. BOLD responses exhibit latency and are not synchronized with stimuli. Prior work uses only past temporal information for decoding. Future temporal context is needed to capture BOLD dynamics.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question concerns whether bi-LSTM improves decoding. The hypothesis is that future context improves BOLD modeling. The hypothesis is that bi-LSTM outperforms unidirectional LSTM. The hypothesis is that no delay adjustment is needed. The predicted outcome is superior accuracy with bi-LSTM. The predicted outcome is accurate representation at every time point.

Methodological Details
The study used working memory fMRI data from the Human Connectome Project. 400 participants were selected from a release of 1200. Participants performed a 2-back working memory task. A 0-back control condition was also included. The task combined category representation stimuli. Four stimulus categories were used. Two runs were available for each participant. Each run had 8 task blocks per task and stimulus combination. Each task block lasted 27.5 seconds. Each scan was a 405 time-point sequence. Preprocessing included field-map distortion correction. Motion variables were regressed out using AFNI. Low-frequency signals were regressed out. Only cortical data was used. The study used 360 cortical regions of interest. Region-averaged timeseries was used as input features. The data was structured as a 360 by 405 tensor. No stimulus-brain-state synchronization was performed. A total of 9 brain states were defined. Fixation blocks were labeled as "others". The bi-LSTM was implemented in Keras. The model was trained on a GeForce GTX 980 GPU. The ADAM optimizer was used with a learning rate of 0.001. The model was trained for 100 epochs. Dropout of 0.3 was applied to prevent overfitting. Class imbalance was handled using Sklearn's compute_class_weight. Inter-subject 10-fold cross-validation was used. The development set was split into 80-20 training-validation sets. The training data was windowed with size 40 and overlap 10.

Procedures And Architectures
Brain-state decoding was modeled as classification. The LSTM defines gated cells for information control. The learning process is called Backpropagation through time. The transition equations define forget, input, cell, and hidden activations. The sigmoid function is used for activation. The bi-LSTM processes data in both directions. The forward hidden activation is computed using past data. The backward hidden activation uses future temporal dependency. The forward and backward activations are combined.
